Cicero. Cicero (Marcus Tullius Cicero, 106 to 43 BCE) was the greatest orator of the Roman Republic and a statesman whose speeches, writings, and political career embodied the ideals of republican virtue. As consul during the conspiracy of Catiline and later as a senator opposing Mark Antony, he defended the Republic against tyranny through rhetoric and law. His work established the classical standard for Latin prose and political philosophy, influencing Western thought for two millennia. Born in Arpinum to an equestrian (non-noble) family, he rose to supreme power through skill in oratory and law rather than aristocratic birth. Elected consul in 63 BCE, he uncovered and defeated the conspiracy of Catiline, a patrician who plotted to overthrow the Republic; his speeches exposing this threat (Catilinarian Orations) became legendary examples of political oratory. Composed the Philippics, fourteen speeches delivered against Mark Antony after the assassination of Julius Caesar, which attacked Antony as a tyrant and defended republican liberty; Antony had him executed for these words. His philosophical writings synthesized Greek Stoicism and Epicureanism for Roman audiences, introducing the via media (middle path) approach to ethics and politics. Perfected the Latin prose style (Ciceronian style) characterized by balanced periods, varied vocabulary, and rhythmic delivery; his works remain the gold standard for rhetorical training. Wrote extensively on rhetoric (De Oratore, Brutus, Orator), defining oratory as the art of persuading audiences through reason, emotion, and character.
